topics.title: Timed Static Contraction (TSC)
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 7 - Variations on the Continuous Tension Protocol/Academy - Variations of the Continuous Tension Protocol 1 - Timed Static Contraction (TSC).txt
topics.moduleLabel: Variations of the Continuous Tension Protocol

blocks.text: As the name implies, a Timed Static Contraction (TSC) is an approach to strength training that involves applying an effort without movement. As such, it is typically safer than a dynamic exercise and can be a good option in situations where a client is dealing with an injury, pain, discomfort, or a return from a surgical procedure. In some cases, it will be better to let a particular joint or muscle heal or for discomfort to subside before attempting to strength train the area. These are typically the more acute variety of injury where there may be some swelling and/or the client has not yet gotten a medical diagnosis. But in situations where there has been chronic or lingering discomfort, AND where there is NO medically advised contraindication to activity, the introduction of careful, static exercise may actually help.

For those clients returning from a surgical procedure (e.g. joint replacement, ligament repair, meniscus procedure, etc), there will usually be a prescribed amount of physical therapy. If the client has not yet finished their physical therapy and therefore does not have medical clearance, we WILL NOT TRAIN OR INVOLVE THE AFFECTED AREA. This is the job of the doctors and physical therapists. They will restore the client back to their normal/acceptable capabilities and we should not disrupt this process. The client may still return to their training with MSF, but we will train around the area and employ additional precautionary measures in selecting movements to ensure the client's safety.

An important distinction between a TSC and a Static Hold (SH), is that with a TSC there is no actual load being held or supported making it quite possibly the safest way to strength train. In order to perform a TSC, there needs to be an immovable movement arm to apply an effort against. This requires setting a given machine so that the movement arm is in the desired position of the range of motion and is held in place either by an amount of weight that cannot be lifted or with a selector pin that abuts the frame and prevents concentric movement.

When determining the static position for the movement arm the instructor must consider and assess where along the range of motion any discomfort or pain may arise. We obviously want to avoid these joint angles at all costs. If a pain free position cannot be found, then we should not choose that particular machine or movement pattern. Furthermore, it is generally safer to use a position that is somewhere near the midpoint of an exercise. The end ranges of motion where the client is either in a lengthened muscle position (i.e. stretched) or a shortened muscle position (i.e. contracted) should be avoided. These positions tend to be either poorly leveraged or overly leveraged and as a result are not as safe. Somewhere near each individual client's midpoint is a safe "starting point" to consider. For single joint exercises and compound pulling movements, it may be beneficial to position the movement arm just beyond the midpoint of the range of motion. So biased toward a slightly more contracted position as the force capabilities diminish in this direction making the exercise inherently safer. In addition, a more contracted position will enhance the "feeling" in the working muscles. And while the sensation of the contraction is not necessarily stimulative, there tends to be a benefit to the mental connection in terms of motor unit recruitment and therefore overall effectiveness of the exercise.
How To Instruct a TSC:

The standard approach is an isometric effort applied for a continuous duration of 90 seconds. This duration is divided into three 30-second intervals. Importantly, if we are instructing an intensity adverse client or one that has a recent injured or repaired joint, the duration used may be shortened. In some cases, intervals as brief as 10 seconds will be the optimal approach for a total of 30 seconds (note: we can use 15, 20, 25-second intervals as well). Safety is always the primary concern and a more conservative introduction of this special method should be considered and discussed internally with the Studio Leader or with MSF Corp.

Regardless of the duration chosen, the instruction and progression through the set will be the same. The first interval is applied with a 50% effort ("Moderate Effort"), the second interval is applied with a 75% effort ("Almost as hard as you can"), and the third with a 100% effort (As hard as you can!"). For this to work properly, the force applied throughout the duration of the exercise must be constant and steady within each interval. The effectiveness, and possibly safety, are diminished if the effort is segmented or applied haphazardly. That makes the instruction even more critical in this situation.

Oftentimes clients will overshoot the beginning of the movement and apply too intense of an effort, which will lead to them having to back off. Then we instruct to increase at the next interval resulting in a situation where there is an inconsistent or undulating on and off sort of effect that obviates the premise of a TSC. We should aim to start the effort slight and build to the greatest effort possible by the end, with a carefully controlled, ever increasing output over the duration. This, like any approach to a physical endeavor, takes practice and it would be better to "under estimate" on the first few attempts to ensure that a gradual increase on the targeted musculature is maintained.

By the time the subject reaches the third interval, their strength is greatly reduced by the first two intervals. Therefore, their ability to produce force is diminished and the now 100% effort required is drastically reduced from what it would be if they were at full strength. This is what contributes to the safety of both the TSC and our MSF Continuous Tension protocol. During TSC, there is no actual load being lifted or supported. As discussed above, this works particularly well for clients with injuries or varying degrees of pain/discomfort as it is the most conservative approach to resistance training. TSC might also help subjects learn to better control and direct their effort with less extraneous muscular involvement. It can also be used to help break the common Valsalva synch. This is due to the fact that muscular and neurological control of dynamic exercise/movement is much more complex than static contraction.

In general, a static approach should almost always be seen as a temporary "bridge" to dynamic exercise. Most people will benefit more from moving during their exercise than they will training statically. Nevertheless, it remains a viable tool in certain situations. If a trainer is not 100% certain on how or when to implement a TSC, they should discuss with their Studio Leader or MSF Corporate for clarification. Static Holds, a closely related method of static exercise are outlined in the following module.

topics.title: Static Hold (SH)
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 7 - Variations on the Continuous Tension Protocol/Academy - Variations of the Continuous Tension Protocol 2 - Static Hold (SH).txt
topics.moduleLabel: Variations of the Continuous Tension Protocol

blocks.text: A closely related method of static strength training to a Timed Static Contraction (TSC) but not as conservative is the Static Hold (SH). While safer than dynamic exercise, it is potentially more risky than a TSC because during a Static Hold, the subject is actually holding or supporting a load. Whereas during a TSC, the subject is producing their own level of force against a movement arm that is locked in place and cannot be moved. Similar to the TSC, a SH can be used in situations where a client is dealing with an injury, pain, discomfort, or a return from a surgical procedure. In some cases, it will be better to let a particular joint or muscle heal or for discomfort to subside before attempting to strength train the area. These are typically the more acute variety of injury where there may be some swelling and/or the client has not yet gotten a medical diagnosis. But in situations where there has been chronic or lingering discomfort, AND where there is NO medically advised contraindication to activity, the introduction of careful, static exercise may actually help.

Static Holds have the benefit of objective feedback in the form of the load being held and the duration of the hold and as such, this method is more easily progressed. But as stated above it is inherently more risky because of this fact. When we actually load the exercise, the client cannot simply use a level of force they are comfortable with, instead they will have to produce a level of force at least high enough to hold or support the load selected. If its a client that has been training with us for a period of time and that has maybe even used the machine dynamically in the past, a reasonable weight selection will be easier to determine. In any case, a discussion with a more senior instructor and/or MSF Corporate is suggested as an extra precaution.

In addition to the weight and duration components to be determined, the highest level of attention must be given to the interpersonal transfer of the load from instructor to client. This is another element of risk that must be managed during a Static Hold that is not a concern during a TSC. During an interpersonal loading transfer, the instructor must first bring the movement arm into position, which is usually near the midpoint on most exercises. The instructor then guides the client to engage the movement arm with the proper part of the body. After affirming proper alignment with the machine, the trainer will instruct the client to begin applying gradual force to the movement arm while the trainer begins to lessen his or her force. The instructor then gradually “hands off” the resistance entirely to the client and pinpoints the completion of the transfer with a clear, concise signal of “yours”.

Static holds for uninjured and otherwise healthy subjects are typically performed with slightly more resistance (+10 to 20%) than the subject would use for a dynamic set. Less weight should be used if we are dealing with an injured or compromised joint. Because of our priority on safety a conservative approach should always be taken. We would much rather use a load that is too light and gradually increase over time than use a load that is too heavy and potentially injurious.

When determining the static position for the movement arm the instructor must consider and assess where along the range of motion any discomfort or pain may arise. We obviously want to avoid these joint angles at all costs. If a pain free position cannot be found, then we should not choose that particular machine or movement pattern. Furthermore, it is generally safer to use a position that is somewhere near the midpoint of an exercise. The end ranges of motion where the client is either in a lengthened muscle position (i.e. stretched) or a shortened muscle position (i.e. contracted) should be avoided. These positions tend to be either poorly leveraged or overly leveraged and as a result are not as safe. Somewhere near each individual client's midpoint is a safe "starting point" to consider. For single joint exercises and compound pulling movements, it may be beneficial to position the movement arm just beyond the midpoint of the range of motion. So biased toward a slightly more contracted position as the force capabilities diminish in this direction making the exercise inherently safer. In addition, a more contracted position will enhance the "feeling" in the working muscles. And while the sensation of the contraction is not necessarily stimulative, there tends to be a benefit to the mental connection in terms of motor unit recruitment and therefore overall effectiveness of the exercise. If possible, the instructor should look to create a hard end stop for the subject to apply their effort against. This is accomplished by placing the selector pin in the stack pin where the selector pin will abut the frame of the weight stack and prevent any further concentric movement. This location will then be recorded in the chart to allow for standardization.
How To Instruct a Static Hold:

During a Static Hold the instructor assists the movement arm (load) to a point in the range of motion where the targeted muscles are loaded and the subject is pain free (see last paragraph for how to configure the machine for use of heavier loads). Ideally this will be somewhere near the client's midpoint of the range of motion. If possible, it is advised that the instructor use a selector pin in the stack pin to create an end stop to apply force against. From this point, the instructor carefully transfers the load over to the client who then attempts to hold that joint angle stationary for time creating tension in the targeted musculature. Failure is achieved when the trainee is unable to prevent negative movement within the constraints of proper form and proper breathing. When first introducing a Static Hold however, the instructor may be advised to avoid true muscular failure and instead look to achieve a time goal of somewhere between 45 to 90 seconds. We should always introduce different exercises and techniques conservatively, especially to a more intensity adverse subject or those with a more recent injury or surgical procedure. With practice and tolerance, the instructor can increase the challenge for the client by increasing load and/or duration but usually not to exceed 120 seconds.

Once the desired duration is achieved, be prepared to take the load away from the client by performing the interpersonal transfer from client to instructor. If the load is considerably heavy to manually control, the machine can be configured so that the distance moved to lift and lower the weight is minimal. This can be accomplished by increasing the gap to the point just before we are to have the client hold the weight. This way the load will only have to be moved an inch or two to lift and lower and the instructor will be spared from having to lift an excessive load. Please consult with MSF Corp or see the video section for more details.

topics.title: Forced Reps
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 7 - Variations on the Continuous Tension Protocol/Academy - Variations of the Continuous Tension Protocol 3 - Forced Reps.txt
topics.moduleLabel: Variations of the Continuous Tension Protocol

blocks.text: NOTE: This technique should be used RARELY and only by a seasoned instructor. There is risk to both the client and the trainer in this situation and an abundance of caution is required. Please discuss with your Studio Leader or MSF Corporate if you are considering this for a particular client.

The most overused “set-extension” technique is the forced rep. This is because of the ease of temptation for its use by any and all trainers. It would seem harmless to employ on the surface but can lead to a dependency, degradation of quality, or injury. As such, forced reps should be a last resort as a means to increase intensity. In some cases a forced rep will keep a client engaged in a set where they would have otherwise reached their maximum tolerable perception of effort and essentially stopping their effort. Their will be temptation on the instructors part to keep the client working but it cannot be stated enough that this technique should not become commonplace. It would be more ideal for the instructor should use encouragement to get the client to increase their effort and push through the sticking point. It would also be more beneficial for the client to understand the need to increase their effort by way of their own volition. This will help them more in the long run as we take them through their life long journey of strength training by using teachable moments.

In any event, if the experienced has decided to use the forced rep technique, they should fully understand how and when to apply it. To perform a forced rep, the instructor applies just enough additional force to assist the trainee in completing the positive phase of the repetition. Once the client has gotten beyond the theoretical “sticking point”, the instructor seamlessly transfers the resistance back to the trainee to continue the repetition themselves. If performed properly the subject should not even notice the assist. It must be reiterated here that forced reps should only be used occasionally if not rarely as the subject will become dependent on or expectant of the assist. This has a tendency to create bad habits and faulty muscular loading patterns. Importantly, only an experienced instructor should consider this technique after acquiring the proper skill and developing keen judgement for its use.

topics.title: Drop Sets
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 7 - Variations on the Continuous Tension Protocol/Academy - Variations of the Continuous Tension Protocol 4 - Drop Sets.txt
topics.moduleLabel: Variations of the Continuous Tension Protocol

blocks.text: A drop set is used to continue the set if a longer duration is desired, as may be the case if the initial resistance selection was too heavy resulting in a very short duration or poor execution. A drop set is performed by briefly pausing to reduce the weight by an appropriate amount after the maximum tolerable perception of effort has been reached to enable the trainee to continue. Importantly, the quality and effect of a workout is entirely up to the instructor to enforce and ensure. Because of this, if the client is struggling to control the weight or they do not feel good about their performance, it will be the instructor's responsibility to make an adjustment and ensure that they themselves and the client are satisfied with each and every set of exercise. While we do not want to get in the habit of having to constantly adjust weights and in a sense "try again," we should do everything in our power to ensure client satisfaction.
